title: Optimistic Updates
description: Make your app feel instant by updating the UI before the server confirms â€” with safe rollback on failure.

data.text: Users expect apps to feel instant. When they click to like a post or archive an email, they should see the change immediately â€” not wait for a round-trip to the server. **Optimistic updates** apply the change to the cache before the request even finishes. If the server responds with an error, React Query rolls back to the previous state. The user gets instant feedback with zero risk of confusing stale UI.

terms.definition: Updating the local cache before the server confirms, giving the user instant feedback.
Restoring the previous cache state if the mutation fails, ensuring the UI is never wrong for long.
The object returned from onMutate that is passed to onError and onSettled, used to carry rollback data.
A QueryClient method that pauses in-flight refetches so an optimistic update is not immediately overwritten.

data.text: Implementing optimistic updates requires three callbacks working together: `onMutate` applies the change and snapshots the old state, `onError` restores the snapshot if the mutation fails, and `onSettled` refetches to guarantee server-side consistency regardless of the outcome.

data.title: The Optimistic Update Steps
items: onMutate: Cancel pending queries, snapshot the current cache, apply the optimistic change, return the snapshot via the context object.
onError: Receive the context object from onMutate and restore the snapshot to roll back the optimistic change.
onSettled: Always refetch the query so the cache reflects the actual server state after the mutation finishes.

data.text: The example below toggles a todo item's completion status. The checkbox ticks instantly. If the PATCH request fails, the checkbox ticks back to its original state without the user noticing anything went wrong.

data.title: Optimistic Toggle with Full Rollback
data.content: A complete useMutation example using onMutate for optimistic update and onError for rollback.

data.title: cancelQueries First
data.text: Always call queryClient.cancelQueries at the start of onMutate. Without it, an in-flight refetch could overwrite your optimistic update before the mutation finishes.

The object returned from `onMutate` is passed through to `onError` and `onSettled` as the third argument. This is the bridge between your optimistic write and your rollback logic. You can pass anything you need â€” the previous cache value, a reference to the updated item, or metadata like the timestamp the action was taken.

data.caption: Flow showing how the context object travels through the optimistic update lifecycle.
data.definition:
sequenceDiagram
    participant U as User
    participant C as Component
    participant QC as QueryClient
    participant API as Server

    U->>C: Clicks toggle
    C->>QC: onMutate fires
    QC->>QC: cancelQueries
    QC->>QC: Snapshot current state
    QC->>QC: setQueryData (optimistic)
    QC-->>C: Return context { previousTodos }
    C->>API: mutationFn executes
    API-->>C: Success response
    C->>QC: onSettled fires
    QC->>API: invalidateQueries (refetch)
    Note over QC,API: If API had errored, onError fires with context
    QC->>QC: setQueryData(previousTodos) rollback

cards.title: Standard Mutation
cards.description: UI updates only after the server confirms the change.
cons: Can feel sluggish on slow connections

cards.title: Optimistic Update
cards.description: UI updates immediately and rolls back on failure.
pros: Great UX for small, frequent actions
cons: UI can flicker briefly on failure

items.question: Should I use optimistic updates for every mutation?
items.answer: No. Use them for quick, frequent actions like toggling a checkbox or liking a post. For heavyweight operations like form submissions, a loading state is usually more appropriate.

items.question: What if the server is wrong and the optimistic update was right?
items.answer: onSettled always invalidates and refetches. After refetch, the cache is updated with the true server state, correcting any discrepancy.

items.question: Can I use optimistic updates with variables from the mutation?
items.answer: Yes. onMutate receives the variables as its first argument. Use it to determine which item to update in the cache.

data.title: Exercise: Optimistic Like Button
data.description: Build a like button that updates the UI instantly and rolls back if the API call fails.
steps: Set up a useQuery to fetch a list of posts.
Create a LikeButton component using useMutation.
In onMutate, cancel the ['posts'] query, snapshot current posts, and toggle the liked count optimistically.
In onError, restore the snapshot if an error occurs.
Show a visual pending state when the mutation is in flight.
Test the rollback by temporarily causing the API to return a 500 error.
data.expectedOutcome: Clicking the like button increments the count instantly. If the request fails, the count silently reverts. After the request settles, the real server value is confirmed via refetch.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Optimistic updates make your app feel instant by updating the cache before the server responds
Always cancel in-flight queries before applying the optimistic change
Return a context object from onMutate so onError can roll back cleanly
Use onSettled to invalidate and refetch, guaranteeing eventual consistency
Use optimistic updates for small, frequent actions â€” not heavyweight form submissions
data.takeaway: Optimistic updates are the secret to snappy, native-feeling web apps. The rollback safety net means users get speed without risk.
